prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

The doubt of future foes exiles my present joy, And wit me warns to shun such snares as threaten mine annoy; For falsehood now doth flow, and subjects’ faith doth ebb, Which should not be if reason ruled or wisdom weaved the web. But clouds of joys untried do cloak aspiring minds, Which turn to rain of late repent by changed course of winds. The top of hope supposed the root upreared shall be, And fruitless all their grafted guile, as shortly ye shall see. The dazzled eyes with pride, which great ambition blinds, Shall be unsealed by worthy wights whose foresight falsehood finds. The daughter of debate that discord aye doth sow Shall reap no gain where former rule still peace hath taught to know. No foreign banished wight shall anchor in this port; Our realm brooks not seditious sects, let them elsewhere resort. My rusty sword through rest shall first his edge employ To poll their tops that seek such change or gape for future joy.

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: The, And, For

outputs.L1:
The uncertainty of future foes banishes my present joy, and wisdom warns me to avoid the snares that threaten my harm. For falsehood now flows freely, and the loyalty of subjects recedes—an order that would not prevail if reason governed, or wisdom wove the web.

Yet clouds of untested joys cloak ambitious minds, only to turn, with shifting winds, into the rain of late repentance. The height of their presumed hope shall be torn up from the root, and all their grafted guile shall prove fruitless, as you shall shortly see.

The eyes dazzled by pride, and blinded by great ambition, shall be opened by worthy persons whose foresight detects falsehood. The daughter of debate, who ever sows discord, shall gain nothing where established rule has long taught the knowledge of peace.

No foreign, banished person shall cast anchor in this port. Our realm does not tolerate seditious sects; let them seek refuge elsewhere. My sword, though rusted by rest, shall first employ its edge to cut down those who seek such change, or who gape after future joy.
outputs.L2:
Concern over enemies yet to come drives away my happiness in the present, and prudence tells me to avoid the traps that may bring me harm. Deceit is now increasing, while the loyalty of subjects is declining—something that would not happen if reason governed events or wisdom shaped their course.

Untested hopes can cover over ambitious hearts like clouds, but when circumstances shift, those hopes will fall like rain into belated regret. The height to which hope has been raised will be torn up from its very roots, and all the cunning they have grafted on will prove barren, as you will soon witness.

Eyes made dim by pride and blinded by great ambition will be opened by honorable people whose foresight can detect deception. The child of argument—discord, which always spreads division—will gain nothing in a place where established rule has long taught peace.

No foreign exile shall find safe harbor here. This kingdom does not tolerate rebellious factions; let them seek refuge somewhere else. My sword, though made rusty by long peace, will first be put back to use by cutting down those who aim for such upheaval or look greedily toward future advantage.
outputs.L3:
Fear of future enemies can easily disturb the happiness of the present. When people allow themselves to be ruled by suspicion and anxiety, they lose the peace they already possess. For this reason, it is necessary to be cautious of harmful deceit and to recognize the danger of those who pretend friendship while secretly preparing mischief. A wise person does not wait until treachery has fully revealed itself, but remains alert to any false appearance that may threaten the common good.

Falsehood and uncertain loyalty have begun to spread because reason and wisdom no longer guide people’s actions. When truth is neglected and judgment is weakened, men become changeable, easily drawn into dishonesty, and ready to abandon the duties they once claimed to honor. Loyalty, which should be firm and constant, becomes unstable when it is not supported by clear understanding and moral discipline. In such a condition, deception grows stronger, and trust among people is placed in danger.

Those who are ambitious and blinded by pride may believe for a time that they can rise through cunning, manipulation, or rebellion. Yet pride often prevents them from seeing the limits of their own power. Their schemes may appear successful at first, but they will eventually be exposed. The hopes they build upon arrogance and deceit will fail, and they will be disappointed when their hidden intentions are brought into the light. No ambition founded on falsehood can remain secure forever.

Discord and sedition will find no lasting place in a realm that is accustomed to peace, order, and stable rule. A people who have long benefited from lawful government are not easily persuaded to exchange security for confusion. The habits of peace, obedience, and mutual trust create a strong defense against disorder. Those who attempt to introduce rebellion into such a realm will discover that unrest cannot easily take root where stability has been deeply established.

For this reason, the speaker declares a firm resolve to oppose anyone who seeks dangerous change or hopes to profit from public unrest. If persuasion and warning are not enough, force will be used against those who threaten the safety of the realm. The peace of the present must be protected from the ambitions of the deceitful, the disloyal, and the rebellious. Those who attempt to disturb the common order will not be allowed to succeed, for the preservation of stability is more important than the schemes of those who seek advantage through disorder.
outputs.L4:
The poem presents a forceful warning against the dangers that can weaken or destroy a realm from within and without. It identifies treachery, reckless ambition, foreign interference, and internal division as serious threats to political order. Rather than treating these dangers as distant or imaginary, the poem insists that they must be recognized clearly and confronted directly. Reason and foresight are shown as essential tools of government: a wise ruler must be able to see through deception, anticipate unrest, and distinguish loyal service from hidden disloyalty. Firm rule is therefore presented not as cruelty, but as a necessary defense against disorder.

At the same time, the poem condemns those who stir up sedition or encourage false hopes among the people. Such figures are portrayed as dangerous because they exploit uncertainty, spread distrust, and seek to undermine lawful authority for their own gain. Foreign influence is also treated with suspicion, especially when it supports rebellion or encourages subjects to betray their country. Against these threats, the poem affirms the strength of the realm and the determination of its ruler. It concludes with confidence that rebellion, deceit, and misguided ambition will ultimately fail. Peace, stability, and lawful government will endure because the ruler remains vigilant, resolute, and committed to preserving the safety of the nation.
outputs.L5:
**The, And, For**

“The,” “and,” and “for” are small words, but they play an important role in English. **The** helps point to something specific, making a sentence clearer. **And** connects ideas, people, or actions, helping thoughts flow together. **For** often shows purpose, reason, or benefit, explaining why something is done or who it is meant to help.

Although these words are simple, they appear everywhere in everyday communication. A sentence like “The book is for Anna and Tom” depends on all three words to make complete sense. Without them, language would feel broken and less natural.

These keywords remind us that even the smallest words can have great value. They support meaning, connect ideas, and make communication easier for everyone.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a 16th-century English court poem in the voice of Queen Elizabeth I, warning ambitious nobles and foreign-backed plotters against rebellion.
counterfactuals.output:
**A Warning from the Crown**

My lords, that climb where fortune’s boughs are thin,  
Take heed what winds about your branches blow;  
The fairest leaves may hide a canker’d sin,  
And highest heads are first laid bare to snow.  

Think not, because my hand in peace is stayed,  
My sword hath lost the memory of steel;  
The lion couchant is not therefore made  
A lamb for every fox to bite at heel.  

What whisper’d gold from over-seas is brought,  
What beads, what bulls, what promises of Spain,  
Shall weigh but light against a kingdom’s thought,  
And purchase nought but hazard, loss, and pain.  

I know the mask, the message, and the sign,  
The midnight oath, the practised saintly face;  
Who drinks to foreign hopes drinks not to mine,  
Nor shall he find my mercy in his place.  

This realm is mine by God and England’s love,  
Not held in fee of priest, nor prince abroad;  
No mitred thunder from the clouds above  
Shall shake the sceptre given me under God.  

Let nobles learn: true honour kneels upright,  
And service is the stair by which men rise;  
But treason, though it plume itself in light,  
Is but a raven black before mine eyes.  

I seek no blood, yet blood shall answer blood  
If subjects turn their daggers on the state;  
Who breaks the bank to let in foreign flood  
Shall drown before he make my people bate.  

Then keep your faith, and I shall keep your name;  
Be loyal, and my grace shall make you great.  
But set one spark to England’s ancient frame,  
And find a queen can both forgive—and fate.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose an Elizabethan-style political verse using archaic diction, rhyming couplets, and themes of treason, false subjects, discord, and a ruler’s resolve to defend the realm.
counterfactuals.output:
When canker’d tongues do whisper treason’s breath,  
And false-heart subjects woo the realm to death,  
When Discord, clad in motley, beats her drum,  
And bids the rabble to rebellion come,  

Then shall the Crown, though hemm’d with storm and spite,  
Stand like a beacon in the murk of night.  
No serpent’s oath, no traitor’s painted plea,  
Shall pluck one jewel from our sovereignty.  

Let perjur’d knaves in shadow’d corners meet,  
And lay their snares beneath the loyal feet;  
The law hath eyes, the throne a tempered hand,  
To purge the rot that would corrupt the land.  

For he that loves not peace, but civil flame,  
Shall win no laurel, only lasting shame.  
And he that serves two masters in his breast  
Shall find no harbour where true hearts have rest.  

Thus speaks our lord, with constancy endued:  
“Though faction howl and malice be renew’d,  
My sword is vow’d, my mercy not made weak—  
I guard the realm for which my people seek.  

Let heaven bear witness, and the earth proclaim:  
No traitor’s craft shall overthrow our name.  
While loyal blood within these borders run,  
The realm stands firm, and treason is undone.”
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a poem that sounds like Tudor-era propaganda against sedition, with phrases about future foes, present joy, falsehood, ambition, and a “rusty sword” ready to punish traitors.
counterfactuals.output:
**A Tudor Warning Against Sedition**

Let every heart in England’s breast  
Be sworn to peace and order blest;  
Let present joy in hall and field  
Be kept beneath our sovereign’s shield.

For future foes may whisper low,  
And plant where honest roses grow  
The weed of falsehood, dark and sly,  
To lift ambition over the sky.

Beware the tongue that flatters sin,  
The smiling face with treason in;  
For he who would the realm divide  
Shall find no mercy for his pride.

The law stands watch by gate and board,  
And in its hand a rusty sword—  
Not idle rust, but wrath delayed,  
For traitors’ necks and rebels made.

Then sing, good folk, with loyal breath,  
“Confusion to the seeds of death!”  
Let sedition’s fire be quenched in shame,  
And England flourish in her name.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Imitate the style of early modern English poetry attributed to Elizabeth I, especially her stern poems about political threats and Mary Queen of Scots, but make it original.
counterfactuals.output:
**A Queen’s Warning**

Though envy creep in velvet shoon,  
And treason mask her face with prayer,  
The sun is not o’ercast at noon  
Because a cloud would climb the air.  

Let whisperers hatch their eggs in night,  
And feed their brood with forged disdain;  
The falcon, hooded, knoweth sight,  
And stoops when time doth bid her reign.  

I wear no crown for idle gold,  
Nor keep a realm by women’s tears;  
The hand that hath the sceptre hold  
Must stop the flood of doubtful fears.  

If cousin’s name be made a snare,  
If pity plead for peril’s breath,  
Shall England sleep, and I forbear,  
Till mercy nurse the child of death?  

No heart more loth than mine to strike,  
No eye more slow to seal a doom;  
Yet weeds and roses grow alike,  
Till judgment give the garden room.  

Let foreign hopes and home-born guile  
Go measure me with softer art:  
I may seem mild a little while,  
But iron keepeth in my heart.  

Who loves my peace, shall have my grace;  
Who shakes my throne, shall learn my will.  
The lion smiles with royal face,  
Yet hath both tooth and talon still.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a Shakespearean/Elizabethan monologue in verse where a monarch rejects foreign exiles and seditious sects, condemns ambition, and threatens to cut down those seeking change.
counterfactuals.output:
**A Monarch’s Rebuke**

What wind hath blown these strangers to our shore,  
These banish’d tongues that murmur at our gates,  
These hungry prophets, lean with foreign dreams,  
Who sell new heavens to purchase earthly thrones?  
Away with them. Our realm is not an inn  
For every fever’d exile’s discontent,  
Nor shall our temples ring with sects and schisms,  
Each petty bell out-clamouring the crown.

I know this sickness—Ambition is its name:  
A gilded worm that feeds within the heart,  
And, being small, would swell to match the sun.  
It kneels, then climbs; it flatters, then commands;  
It calls its treason “conscience,” “right,” and “change,”  
And masks a dagger in a preacher’s sleeve.  
O, I have seen how alteration breeds:  
First whispers in the alehouse, then a crowd,  
Then banners, drums, and fathers slain by sons,  
Till law lies strangled in the market-place.

Shall I, anointed, set upon this seat  
By time, by blood, by heaven’s awful hand,  
Be lesson’d by thin men with pamphlet tongues?  
Shall every malcontent that lost his roof  
Abroad, come hither to unthatch mine own?  
No. Let them find some colder star to serve,  
Some prince more soft, some kingdom ripe for fire;  
Here stands a crown that will not bend to smoke.

And you, my lords, whose eyes begin to shine  
With borrowed dawns—take heed. The tree of state  
Hath branches high, but roots are under earth;  
Who hacks the root shall fall beneath the bough.  
I’ll have no pruning by rebellious hands,  
No gardener’s knife where subjects judge the king.  
If change must come, it shall come down from me,  
As thunder comes from heaven, not from dust.

Therefore proclaim: who stirs the people’s blood,  
Who harbours banish’d wolves, or feeds these sects,  
Who names ambition “virtue,” and calls peace  
A prison built by kings to cage the brave—  
Let him beware the sickle of the law.  
For I will cut such springing mischiefs short,  
Crop head from stalk, and make the field lie plain,  
Till every blade remember who is sun,  
And who but grass beneath a monarch’s tread.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
